blocks.text: Rating scales give clinicians an objective benchmark to support critical treatment decisions; regular use can aid diagnosis, prognosis and therapeutic monitoring. With self-report scales, item-by-item analysis can identify the exact symptoms the patient finds most troublesome so they can be targeted in consultation.

Rating scales can be used for (1) screening for a psychiatric condition, (2) diagnosis of a psychiatric illness (such scales are often termed diagnostic schedules), (3) estimating severity of conditions and their response to treatment, and (4) assessing functional capacity and well-being.
Rating scales can be self-rated or observer rated. Some observer-rated scales need clinical experience (clinician-rated); trained non-clinical personnel can use others.

Scales are based on psychometric properties and aim to measure dimensions of psychopathology (symptoms), often at the present state. Schedules are based on clinical expectations and deal with categories of disorders (syndromes) based on known classification systems; a schedule may focus on past or present status or both.

Two procedures are used to select scale items. The first is based on the previous clinical literature. The second is calibration: a large number of questions are tested to find the most discriminating items between a known ill and a presumed well group, and the statistically most significant items are chosen.

blocks.title: Considerations when selecting a screening measure
rows: Characteristics of the population to be screened
Time required to complete the measure

blocks.text: The General Health Questionnaire (**GHQ**) is an all-purpose screening tool, often used as a first-level assessment instrument in epidemiological studies before detailed diagnostic schedules are employed. It was introduced by Goldberg to detect those likely to have, or be at risk of developing, psychiatric disorders.

blocks.title: General Health Questionnaire (GHQ) key facts
rows: 12, 28, 30 or 60 items; the 28-item version is used most widely
Each item scored 0-3, so **GHQ-28** total is 0 to 84
Least symptomatic items 0, most symptomatic 1; 28- and 30-item versions: score exceeding 4 = psychiatric caseness
A probabilistic term: such respondents presenting in general practice would likely receive further attention
Not usually used for predictive purposes

blocks.text: The **GHQ-28** maximum score is 84 (0-3 per item): the options include 28 and 12, which are the item count and the shortest version, plus 42 and 72 - do not answer with the number of items.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

items.text: The **GHQ** is the self-rated screening instrument for the presence of psychiatric illness (not **GAF**, Quality of Life Interview, Structured Clinical Interview or Diagnostic Interview Schedule).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

items.text: The **GHQ** is the questionnaire for identifying psychiatric caseness in the general population (not **BDI**, **HAM-D**, **SCID-5** or **SCAN**).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

items.text: The **GHQ** is the scale usable by primary care physicians, general medical professionals and in community studies (not **SAPS**, **SANS**, Simpson-Angus or **BPRS**).

bullets.text: Rating scales: screening, diagnosis (diagnostic schedules), severity/treatment response, functional capacity and well-being.
Self-rated: BDI, Zung, SCL, GHQ, Lunser, EPDS. Observer rated: dementia scales, PANSS, BPRS, HAMD, MADRS, YBOCS, SCID.
Item selection: from clinical literature, or by calibration (most discriminating items between known ill and presumed well).
GHQ (Goldberg): first-level screening in epidemiological studies; versions 12/28/30/60, GHQ-28 most used.
GHQ-28 Likert 0-3 gives max 84; binary scoring caseness is a score above 4 (3 for GHQ-12).

blocks.title: Diagnostic schedules
rows: Revised version for lay interviewers (**CIS-R**). Used in National Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys of Great Britain. Developed by Goldberg et al. Identifies common disorders in primary care and community settings (focus on neurotic conditions)
Incorporates principles of both **PSE** and **DIS**. Produced by **WHO** for use with both **ICD** and **DSM** diagnoses
Used in **ECA** study. Lifetime **DSM** diagnoses made initially; a time period can later be specified for current diagnoses
Trained primary care workers (**HSCL-25**) or self-reported (original)

58-item self-report version measures neurotic symptom distress in outpatients; 25-item version measures anxiety (10 items) and depression (15 items). **SCL-90R** and Brief Symptom Inventory (**BSI**) are derivatives

Self-report version of **PRIME-MD** (Spitzer et al., based on **DSM-III**); diagnoses common neurotic conditions in primary care. **PHQ-9** focuses on the 9 **DSM-IV** depression criteria; **GAD-7** on anxiety; **PHQ-15** on depression with somatic features
Provides clinical diagnoses along the lines of the **ICD** system. **CATEGO** is the computerised version of **PSE**
Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (**SADS**)
Covers depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders. Regular, lifetime and change versions; children version is Kiddie-**SADS**
Developed by Wing et al. on the basis of **PSE** and has replaced **PSE** at present. Focused on adult psychopathology; 28 sections and 1872 items (many can be skipped)
For patients in whom a psychiatric diagnosis is suspected. Non-patient version for epidemiological studies. **SCID-II** is for axis 2 disorders

blocks.title: General observations on diagnostic schedules
rows: Most schedules are either **DSM** or **ICD** based; only a few cater to both
A number of primary-care oriented schedules focus largely on nonpsychotic disorders
Many have computerised forms, but a number are time-consuming to complete routinely or at initial clinical contact
Almost all are clinician-administered, though self-report forms have evolved recently

blocks.text: **SCID** is the most reliable instrument for a clinical diagnosis according to **DSM** criteria - the distractors are **AIMS** (a movement scale), **SCAN**, **HAMD** (a rating scale) and **MMPI**.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **SCID** is primarily used in research with trained interviewers (clinician-administered, semi-structured) - **NOT** for untrained lay interviewers, **NOT** dimensional, **NOT** tied to **ICD-10** and it does not provide the **DSM-IV** Axis V diagnosis.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **SCAN** is the schedule that has replaced the Present State Examination (it evolved from the **PSE**); **PANSS**, **SSPI**, **CASH** and **SANS** are the distractors.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **PSE** is the scale that retains the aspects of a mental state examination during the consultation - the distractors HoNOS, **CATEGO**, **SANS** and **BPRS** do not (**CATEGO** is only the computerised **PSE**).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: CIS: fully structured, clinician-administered, neurotic conditions in primary care/community; CIS-R for lay interviewers; used in UK Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys.
CIDI: WHO schedule combining PSE and DIS principles, for ICD and DSM. DIS: non-clinician-administered, fully structured, used in ECA study.
HSCL: 58-item self-report; HSCL-25 = anxiety (10) + depression (15); SCL-90R and BSI derive from it.
PHQ is the self-report version of PRIME-MD; PHQ-9 = 9 DSM-IV depression criteria, GAD-7 anxiety, PHQ-15 somatic depression.
PSE: clinician semi-structured, ICD-style diagnoses (CATEGO = computerised). SCAN (Wing) replaced PSE; 28 sections, 1872 items.
SADS: major mental illnesses with regular/lifetime/change versions; Kiddie-SADS for children. SCID: DSM-IV, SCID-II for axis 2.
Most schedules are DSM- or ICD-based, many focus on nonpsychotic disorders, almost all clinician-administered.

blocks.text: The 2 Questions scale (**PHQ-2**): an affirmative response to (1) "Over the past two weeks, have you ever felt down, depressed, or hopeless?" and (2) "Have you felt little interest or pleasure in doing things?" may be as effective as longer screening measures or may indicate the need for in-depth diagnostic tools.

blocks.title: Adult depression scales
rows: 17-21 items (2 versions); refers to last 1-2 weeks; more items for biological features; remains a reference standard

Max score 63; last 2 weeks; 0-13 minimal, 14-19 mild, 20-28 moderate, >28 severe; lacks discriminatory power among very severely ill; more psychological than somatic factors; can be repeated at short intervals
Avoids imbalance towards psychological factors seen in Beck; poor correlation with observer rating; insensitive to change
Easiest way to quantify depression severity; patient indicates state of mood on the line

blocks.text: Children: depression screening is generally appropriate in children at least seven years of age. The Reynolds Child Depression Scale and the Children's Depression Inventory (full version 27 items; screening version 10 items) were developed specifically for children and are written at lower reading levels.

**BDI** is the adult depression scale the question keys as validated in children aged 14 and older - but the explanation itself says it can screen from age 13 (a number to hold loosely); Cornell, Edinburgh, Clifton and Wechsler are the distractors.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: For screening depression in adolescents aged 14-18 the answer is the **BDI** (a self-report measure) - not the clinician-completed Hamilton or **SCID**, nor the Child Behaviour Checklist or **CAFAS**.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Advantages of the **BDI** and **CES-D** include ease of scoring, low cost and comparable psychometric properties. The **MFQ** is endorsed by **NICE** and has self and parent-rated versions.
The **BDI** has more cognitive items than Hamilton, Montgomery-Asberg, **GHQ** or Young - the explanation says it focuses on behavioural and cognitive dimensions of depression.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **BDI** true statement is 21 items; the distractors are symptoms over the last five days (the explanation says the last 2 weeks), maximum score 42, no item on suicidal ideas, and strictly clinician-rated (it is self-rated).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Montgomery-Asberg is the depression scale most sensitive to change - the distractors **VAS**, **BDI**, Zung and **HADS** are not; like Hamilton its 10-item version needs a clinical interview.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Simpson-Angus is the odd one out among mood scales: Beck, Hamilton, Montgomery-Asberg and Young rate mood, whereas Simpson-Angus detects and monitors extrapyramidal symptoms.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **BDI** is the self-report measure; Abbreviated Mental Test, Glasgow Coma Scale, Hamilton and Clinical Global Improvement are not self-report.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Perinatal depression: the **BDI**, **CES-D** and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (**EPDS**) have been used to screen in antepartum and postpartum periods. The **BDI** and **CES-D** tend to produce higher scores and more false-positive results in symptomatic pregnant women.

The **EPDS** was specifically developed for postpartum depression and relies much less on somatic questions. It has 10 items (self or clinician-rated), framed within the "past seven days" with a frequency-based response format. Routine use of **EPDS** postpartum has been shown to increase detection compared with usual care.

Geriatric depression: the Geriatric Depression Scale (**GDS**) was developed for geriatric patients and has fewer somatic items; questions pertain to the past week and responses are only "yes" or "no". With cognitive deficits, interviewer-administered instruments such as the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia or the Hamilton scale are preferred.

The Cornell measure should be administered to the patient's primary caregiver. **BASDEC** (Brief Assessment Schedule Depression Cards) is designed for general hospital use and stops questions being overheard on geriatric wards; patients choose answers from a deck of 19 cards presented one at a time.

Depression in schizophrenia: most depression scales are tuned to non-psychotic patients and contain items that do not distinguish depressed from non-depressed psychotic patients (e.g. delusions of nihilism). The Calgary Depression Scale for Schizophrenia (**CDSS**) focuses on depressive symptoms in the presence of schizophrenia.

blocks.note: The notes say the **BDI** includes "more psychological than somatic factors"; the question explanation adds that it focuses on behavioural and cognitive dimensions and that the current version added coverage of somatic symptoms. The notes do not mention the added somatic coverage.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.note: The notes give **BDI** bands of 20-28 moderate and >28 severe and an age appropriateness of 14 and older. The explanation to this question instead says a score of >17 indicates moderate and >30 severe depression, and that the **BDI** can screen from age 13 and older. Check which figures a question uses.

bullets.text: PHQ-2: two questions (down/depressed/hopeless; little interest or pleasure) over the past two weeks.
HAMD: observer rated, 17-21 items, last 1-2 weeks, reference standard. MADRS: 10 items, most sensitive to change.
BDI: self-rated 21 items, max 63, bands 0-13/14-19/20-28/>28; more psychological than somatic; Zung: 20 items, self-rated, insensitive to change.
VAS: 10 cm line, easiest way to quantify depression severity.
Child/adolescent: screening from age 7; CDI 7-17, MFQ 8-18 (NICE-endorsed), Reynolds Child 8-12, Reynolds Adolescent 13-18, BDI and CES-D 14+.
EPDS: 10 items, past 7 days, little reliance on somatic items; BDI and CES-D give more false positives in pregnancy.
Elderly: GDS (yes/no, past week, fewer somatic items); Cornell or Hamilton preferred in cognitive deficit.
Cornell given to the primary caregiver; BASDEC 19 cards for general hospital use. Schizophrenia: CDSS.
Question explanation gives BDI moderate >17 and severe >30 and screening from age 13 (notes: 20-28, >28, age 14+).

blocks.title: Alcohol rating scales
rows: 4 questions: cutting down; annoyed/criticised; bad or guilty; eye-opener. A positive answer should raise suspicion of an alcohol problem, a score of 2 is highly suggestive. Takes under a minute

10 items: quantity, frequency, inability to control drinking, withdrawal relief, loss of memory, injury, concern by others. Score 8+ = harmful/hazardous drinking; 13+ in women and 15+ in men = dependent drinking. Widely used; recommended by **WHO** for primary care
Simple self-report 25-item yes/no test. Score 3-5 early indicator of problem drinker; 6+ highly likely problem drinker. Brief **MAST** uses 10 items; G-**MAST** and Brief G-**MAST** for older people

Rates severity of alcohol withdrawal; 10 items, 9 scored 0-7 and one 0-4 (total 67). Can be used regularly day and night to assess withdrawal and treatment impact. Covers nausea, tremor, paroxysmal sweating, anxiety, agitation, auditory/visual/tactile disturbances, headache, orientation

blocks.forTopic: The four alcohol scales (CAGE, AUDIT, MAST, CIWA)

expansion: Eye-opener: first drink in the morning to steady nerves or hangover

blocks.text: **SCOFF** is the odd one out among **MAST**, **AUDIT**, **CAGE** and **CIWA**: **SCOFF** is a screening tool for eating disorders, not an alcohol assessment tool.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **SCOFF** is the answer for early detection of an eating disorder - the distractors Prochaska, **AUDIT**, **CAMCOG** and **CAGE** are alcohol or other tools (**CAGE** is the alcohol analogue of the **SCOFF** mnemonic).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.note: A question asks the **SAWS** cut-off for pharmacotherapy; the explanation says mild withdrawal is under 12 and moderate to severe withdrawal (requiring intervention) is 12 or more. **SAWS** is not described in the notes (only **CIWA** is).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: CAGE: 4 questions, under a minute; positive answer raises suspicion, score of 2 highly suggestive.
AUDIT: 10 items; 8+ harmful/hazardous; 13+ women and 15+ men dependent; WHO-recommended for primary care.
MAST: 25 yes/no items; 3-5 early problem drinker, 6+ highly likely; Brief MAST 10 items; G-MAST for older people.
CIWA: rates withdrawal severity, 10 items (9 scored 0-7, one 0-4, total 67), repeatable day and night.

blocks.title: Child psychiatry scales
rows: Assesses degree of impairment in functioning due to emotional, behavioural or psychiatric problems. Completed by clinical staff in about 10 minutes. Useful for outcome over time and directing case management. Measures aggression and conduct problems, especially ages 7 to 17

Records behavioural problems and competencies of children aged 4 through 16 as reported by parents or others who know the child well. 113 items, Likert scale. Gives a total score plus internalizing (fearful, shy, anxious, inhibited) and externalizing (aggressive, antisocial, undercontrolled) scores. Self-administered or by interview; can measure change over time or after treatment. Teacher Report Forms, Youth Self-Reports and Direct Observation Forms exist. Two versions: ages 1 1/2 - 5 and 6 - 18
Originally developed in the early 1990s; fully structured diagnostic interview for **DSM**-based diagnoses in children

Family of instruments measuring a range of childhood psychopathology; most commonly used in assessment of **ADHD**. Teacher, parent and self-report (adolescents) versions; short and long (up to 80 items) forms

bullets.text: CAFAS: clinician-completed (~10 min) impairment scale, aggression and conduct problems, ages 7 to 17; tracks outcome.
CBCL: 113 items, ages 4-16 (versions 1 1/2-5 and 6-18), parent/other reported; total, internalizing and externalizing scores.
DISC: fully structured DSM-based diagnostic interview for children.
Conners: family of scales, most used for ADHD; teacher, parent and self-report versions.

sections.title: 6. Scales used in old age psychiatry

blocks.title: Cognitive and dementia scales in old age
rows: Widely used to measure psychopathology in community surveys of the elderly. **AGECAT** is a computerised algorithm based on **GMSS**

Popular cognitive screening instrument; 10 minutes by a trained interviewer; suggested cut-off 23 for cognitive impairment; educational status affects scores; does not pick up frontal lobe deficits; moderate to minimal sensitivity to change in mild cognitive impairment
10-point questionnaire of memory and orientation in 3 minutes; origins in Blessed Dementia Scale; cut-off 7/8 out of 10 suggests cognitive impairment

Cognitive and non-cognitive assessment, 45 minutes by trained professional; cognitive section is **ADAS**-Cog; gold standard for measuring change in cognitive function in anti-dementia drug trials; a fall of about ==10%== per year is expected in Alzheimer's disease

Severity of behavioural symptoms of dementia over ten domains (delusions, hallucinations, dysphoria, anxiety, agitation/aggression, euphoria, disinhibition, irritability/lability, apathy, aberrant motor behaviour); scored 1 to 144; severity and frequency independently assessed

blocks.title: Behavioural, carer-rated and disability scales in old age
rows: Clinician-administered; documents behavioural symptoms in Alzheimer's disease: paranoid and delusional ideation, hallucinations, activity disturbances, aggression, diurnal variation, mood, anxieties and phobias
Manchester and Oxford Universities Scale for the Psychopathological Assessment of Dementia; administered to carers by an experienced clinician to measure **BPSD**
Clifton Assessment Procedure for the Elderly (**CAPE**; Pattie & Gilleard, 1979)

Assesses level of disability and estimates need for care. Short cognitive scale plus behavioural rating scale with four sub-scales: physical disability, apathy, communication difficulties, social disturbance. Quick and easy to administer
Bristol Activities of Daily Living Scale
Assesses 20 daily living abilities in dementia; caregiver-rated; designed for community use by trained health professionals

blocks.text: **MMSE** is the most commonly used screening tool for dementia in older people - its explanation gives a cut-off of 24/30 and 5-10 minutes, whereas the notes give a cut-off of 23 and 10 minutes; check which figure a question uses.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The Clifton Assessment Procedure (**CAPE**) is used in residential care for the elderly - the distractors are schizophrenia rehabilitation, foster care, learning disability care homes and prisons; it assesses disability and need for care.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: GMSS: community surveys of elderly; AGECAT is its computerised algorithm.
MMSE: 10 min, cut-off 23, education-dependent, misses frontal deficits, poor sensitivity to change in mild impairment.
AMTS: 10 points, 3 minutes, cut-off 7/8 (Hodkinson 1972).
ADAS-Cog: gold standard for change in cognition in anti-dementia trials; about 10% fall per year expected in Alzheimer's.
NPI: ten behavioural domains, scored 1-144. BEHAVE-AD: clinician-administered behavioural symptoms. MOUSEPAD: carer-administered BPSD scale.
CAPE: disability and need for care; cognitive scale plus four-sub-scale behaviour rating.
Bristol ADL: 20 daily living abilities in dementia, caregiver-rated.

blocks.title: Other clinical rating scales
rows: Severity and monitoring of change in schizophrenia; 30 items covering positive symptoms, negative symptoms and general psychopathology
Rates severity in patients with a pre-existing diagnosis of **OCD**
567 questions covering 8 areas of psychopathology, 2 additional personality-type areas and 3 scales assessing truthfulness; compared with normative non-clinical data. Not a projective test
67 standardised probe questions; 57-item true/false screening questionnaire also included; produces **ICD-10** personality disorder diagnosis
Two items: **CGI-S** (severity, current condition, 1-7) and **CGI-I** (improvement since start of treatment, 1-7); any psychiatric disorder in clinic or ward
Rated by physician on semi-structured interview (18 items, 7 points each, max 108)

Developed by Overall, 1960; one of the most widely used clinical rating scales; originally for controlled trials of new psychotropics; includes observations and patient reports. Factor analysis yields five factors: hostility-suspiciousness, withdrawal-retardation, thinking disturbance, depression-anxiety, activation

Not diagnostic devices; used in studies of neurobiological correlates of symptom groupings. **SAPS** 34 items (hallucinations, delusions, bizarre behaviour, formal thought disorder); **SANS** 25 items (affective flattening/blunting, alogia, apathy, asociality, inattention)

99 true-false items; follow-up Clinical Significance Scale interview checks the trait is enduring (criterion D), present without other disorders (criteria E and F) and causes distress/impairment (criterion C)

blocks.title: SCOFF questions (eating disorder screen)
rows: Do you make yourself **SICK** when you feel uncomfortably full?
Do you worry you have lost **CONTROL** over how much you eat?
Have you recently lost more than 14 pounds (**ONE** stone) within three months?
Do you believe you are **FAT** when others say you are too thin?
Would you say that **FOOD** dominates your life?

blocks.text: **SCOFF** is a mnemonic for eating disorder screening (similar to **CAGE** for alcohol); it has high sensitivity (2 or more questions positive).

**BPRS** correct statement is global psychiatric symptomatology - the distractors are a 6-point item rating, a negative-symptom focus, a 30-item scale and self-administration; the explanation says 18 or 24 items rated on 7-8 points, clinician-rated (the notes state 18 items, 7 points each).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **BPRS**: the options 'cannot be used to detect treatment response' and 'requires no clinical training' are false - it is an outcome measure in treatment studies and reliability needs substantial rater training; 20 and 8 items are wrong (18 or 24).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: A young man with voices discussing him and thought control needs a symptom-severity scale - **BPRS** is the key; **SANS** is negative-symptom only and **GHQ** is a screen, so they are distractors.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Delusions of cameras spying, withdrawal and voices - **PANSS** (clinician-administered, severity and change in schizophrenia) is the answer; **MADRS**, **MMSE**, **HAS** and **GHQ** are distractors.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **HAM-D** is the exception among projective tests - Rorschach, Sentence Completion, Draw-a-Person and **TAT** are projective but **HAM-D** is not (the notes add that **MMPI** is not projective either).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **AIMS** is the scale for drug-induced movement abnormalities in general and tardive dyskinesia in particular (12 items, clinician-administered) - not Barnes Akathisia, Simpson-Angus, Lane or **LUNSERS**.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Lane scale is the scale that is **NOT** for drug-induced movement abnormalities (it is for minor physical anomalies); **LUNSERS**, Barnes Akathisia, Simpson-Angus and **AIMS** are.

items.text: **BPRS**, a clinician-rated observation scale, is most commonly used in schizophrenia (not alcohol use disorder, personality disorder, bipolar disorder or somatisation disorder).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Rating Scales Attempt review.pdf

items.text: For measuring severity and change in psychotic symptoms the answer is **BPRS** (not **NPI**, **CATEGO**, Young mania or **SCAN**).

Questions state **AIMS** is a 12-item clinician-administered scale for antipsychotic side effects including tardive dyskinesia; Simpson-Angus rates 10 items 0-4 for extrapyramidal symptoms; the Lane scale is for minor physical anomalies, so it is not a drug-induced movement scale.

bullets.text: PANSS: clinician-administered, 30 items (positive, negative, general psychopathology) for schizophrenia severity/change. Y-BOCS: severity in known OCD.
SCOFF: eating disorder screen (like CAGE); sick, control, one stone, fat, food; 2+ positive = high sensitivity.
MMPI: 567 self-report questions, 8 psychopathology areas, 2 personality areas, 3 truthfulness scales; NOT a projective test.
IPDE: semi-structured, 67 probe questions, ICD-10 personality diagnoses. CGI: CGI-S and CGI-I, both scored 1-7.
BPRS (Overall, 1960): 18 items, 7 points each, max 108; five factors incl. hostility-suspiciousness and thinking disturbance.
SAPS 34 items / SANS 25 items: not diagnostic, used for neurobiological correlates. PDQ-4+: 99 true-false items for 12 DSM-IV personality disorders.
BPRS: global symptomatology, clinician-rated, 18 or 24 items on 7-8 points; not negative-symptom, 30-item or self-administered.

blocks.text: Treatment outcomes are multidimensional rather than single constructs. Outcome measures are classified broadly into five types.

blocks.title: Types of outcome measure
rows: Individual symptom severity; can also give relapse/remission measures
Overall appraisal of disease severity and impact on overall functioning
Several domains of health-related quality of life, applicable irrespective of illness
Several domains of health-related quality of life for specific patient groups
A specific domain, e.g. social function, interpersonal relationships, cognitive capacity or service satisfaction

blocks.title: Criteria for a useful outcome measure
rows: Is it appropriate to the question addressed by the trial or the benefit desired by the service?
Reproducible, internally consistent, precise and accurately reflecting the construct?
Scores intuitively meaningful and comparable to real-life states?
Readily applicable in clinical settings and not too onerous on clinicians and patients?

blocks.forTopic: Five criteria for a useful outcome measure

blocks.title: Examples of outcome scales
rows: Appendix to **DSM-IV**; overall psychosocial functioning on a 10-item (100-point) scale from self-report and clinical interview; used in axis V of **DSM-IV** multiaxial system; combines symptom severity and functional impairment, based on clinician appraisal of functional limitation

Proposed as new axis in Appendix B of **DSM-IV**; related to **GAF** but focuses only on functioning, not symptoms; does not discriminate psychiatric from non-psychiatric causes; clinician-rated on a 100-point scale with descriptors per 10-point interval; guided tools include the Personal and Social Performance scale (**PSP**)
Clinical practice, research, policy evaluation, community surveys; self-administered from age 14 up or by trained interviewer; eight health concepts

Most widely used psychiatric outcome scale in the **NHS**; developed by RCPsych, commissioned by Department of Health in 1993; 12 items measuring behaviour, impairment, symptoms and social functioning, from routine clinical assessments

blocks.title: The eight SF-36 health concepts
rows: Limitations in physical activities because of ill health
Limitations in social activities because of physical or emotional problems
Limitations in role performance due to physical health problems
Limitations in role performance because of emotional problems

bullets.text: Five outcome measure types: psychopathological rating scale, global, generic patient-based, disease-specific, domain-specific.
Useful outcome measure: appropriate, reliable and valid, responsive, readily interpretable, acceptable and feasible.
GAF: DSM-IV axis V, combines symptoms and function. SOFAS: function only, not symptoms, 100 points, PSP is a guided tool.
SF-36: generic quality-of-life measure, 8 concepts, self-administered from age 14.
HoNOS: most widely used NHS outcome scale; RCPsych 1993; 12 items.

blocks.text: Two properties matter when developing scales: validity (does the scale measure the actual phenomenon?) and reliability (does it give consistent results?). Reliability is the replicable nature of tools; high reliability guarantees consistency but not scientific validity.

blocks.title: Types of reliability
rows: Instrument administered twice to the same population
Interval long enough to avoid practice effect but short enough that the state does not change; 2 to 14 days often used in psychiatry
Correlates each item with the total score and averages the correlations
Values from negative infinity to 1 but only positive values make sense; arbitrary cut-off 0.70
Scale split into two parts and correlation examined
Two or more raters rate the same population with the same scale

Intraclass correlation coefficient (**ICC**) for continuous variables: 0 (unreliable) to 1 (perfect); 0.6 fair, 0.8 very good, 0.9 excellent; relative **ICC** always higher than absolute **ICC**; **ANOVA** **ICC** for >2 raters/groups. Kappa or weighted kappa for nominal data with more than two categories

blocks.title: Types of validity
rows: Subjective judgment whether the test measures the construct on its face
Hamilton depression scale has face value for depression, not for obsessions
Whether the test really measures the theoretical construct of interest; unified construct validity = content + criterion validity
Whether each subscale/item fits what the test was designed to measure; good coverage of all domains; cannot often be statistically tested, experts comment
Performance against an external criterion (concurrent or predictive)
Distinguishes subjects who differ concurrently on other measures
High on insomnia scale may score high on fatigue scale
Predicts future group differences from current score differences
High childhood aggression score and adult criminal incidents
Predicts or explains variance over and above other measures
Agreement between instruments measuring the same construct
Disagreement between scales measuring different constructs
Poor correlation between **HAMD** and Hamilton Anxiety scale
Sensitivity to change: must show a difference when an intervention modifies the domain
Form of construct validity established via factor analysis of items

blocks.title: Validity: the question each type answers
rows: Does this scale appear fit for the purpose of measuring the variable of interest?
Does this scale appear to include all the important domains of the measured attribute?
Is the scale consistent with what we already know (concurrent) and what we expect (predictive)?
Does this new scale associate with a different scale measuring a similar construct?
Does the new scale disagree with scales measuring unrelated constructs?

blocks.text: 'Interrater validity' is the false option among types of validity (face, construct, ecological, content): inter-rater agreement is a reliability, not a validity.

blocks.text: Construct validity is tested by whether the constituent parts of the questionnaire are suitable and related to the phenomenon; predicting the future, covering most symptoms, same results on retest by one rater or by two raters are the distractors.

blocks.text: Precision is how much a calculated central value (e.g. mean) varies with repeated sampling; narrower variation means more precision, and random errors cause imprecision. Factors reducing precision include wider interval limits and expecting a higher confidence interval (==99.7%== vs ==95%==). Accuracy is how close the mean is to the true population value. Precision is comparable to reliability, accuracy to validity; bias compromises validity/accuracy.

bullets.text: Reliability = consistency (high reliability does not guarantee validity); validity = measures what it proposes to measure.
Test-retest interval 2-14 days; Cronbach's alpha internal consistency cut-off 0.70; split-half; interrater (ICC, kappa).
ICC: 0 to 1; 0.6 fair, 0.8 very good, 0.9 excellent; kappa or weighted kappa for nominal data.
Face (subjective), content (domain coverage, expert judgment), criterion (concurrent/predictive), construct (unified = content + criterion).
Convergent: same construct agrees (BDI-HAMD); discriminant: different constructs disagree (HAMD vs Hamilton Anxiety); experimental: sensitivity to change.
Precision ~ reliability (random error); accuracy ~ validity (bias).

blocks.text: Risk is the likelihood that harm will occur. Risk assessment is a process of scientific (statistical/clinical) calculation of the likelihood of an adverse event. Risk management is integral to assessment; assessment is not for labelling people but is dynamic and specific to the event of importance. Risk cannot be eliminated, only reduced.

blocks.title: Problems with predicting risk
rows: Events of interest are rare, so predictive value is low; serious violence among the severely mentally disordered is under ==1%== (Wallace 1998); false positive rate of even a very good instrument compromises predictive utility
Risk depends on several factors that change over time
Comprehensive evaluations are time-consuming; interaction among factors is often unknown

blocks.title: Static, stable and dynamic risk factors (Bouch & Marshall, 2003)
rows: Fixed and historical; cannot be modified
Long-term, enduring but modifiable to some extent
Fluctuate markedly in duration and intensity; can act synergistically and multiply effect of static and stable factors if not addressed promptly

blocks.text: A comprehensive risk assessment considers static, stable, dynamic and future risk factors (certain dynamic factors may occur only in future, e.g. feeling helpless on discharge) and includes them in risk management strategies.

blocks.title: Approaches to risk assessment
rows: Subjective, intuitive judgment informed by experience; opinions highly variable with poor predictive value; most risk assessment currently done this way; only 1/3 of pure clinical judgments estimated correct in retrospective studies

Formal, algorithmic, objective; numerical probability of future outcome; very popular in forensic services; superior for violence and sexual offending; does not inform which risk factors to target; hardly any tools for self-harm/suicide, many for violence

Combines evidence base for risk factors with individual clinical assessment; structured scales-based assessment when formulating risk management plan; e.g. **HCR-20** for violence in forensic settings

blocks.title: Problems of actuarial tools
rows: Historical aspects given more importance, so a pessimistic view of risk, insensitive to change
Hard to generalise tools developed in one setting to another
Too focused on static and stable rather than dynamic, modifiable factors

blocks.text: Actuarial instruments identify at-risk groups more accurately, but structured risk instruments may be more clinically useful for clinical decision-making. Neither actuarial nor structured judgments should replace conventional clinical assessment; they are additional aids to systematically identify and address relevant risk factors.

blocks.title: Stages in risk assessment and management (Bouch & Marshall)
rows: Identify need for a full structured risk assessment (not everyone needs this)
Assess static, stable, dynamic and future risk factors and consider protective factors
Individual formulation of risk applied to the current presentation
Consider possible interventions and the level of support required
Anticipate the impact of possible interventions
Develop a management plan with specified short and long-term implementations
Review and revise the management plan as risk factors vary

blocks.text: **HCR-20** is a popular structured clinical tool for violence risk with good inter-rater reliability; it has been useful in predicting inpatient violence and community violence in discharged patients.

blocks.title: Other structured risk tools
rows: Spousal assault risk assessment guide; 20 risk factors; gauges future violence risk in men arrested for spousal assault
Sexual violence risk scale; 20 items for assessing violence risk in sex offenders
10 major demographic risk factors in a mnemonic to assess immediate suicide risk, often in acute general hospital; scores guide admit/discharge
20 true-false statements on pessimism about the future; scores 0-3 minimal, 4-8 mild, 9-14 moderate, 15-20 severe risk
Self-report, 24 items (5 screening items); thoughts, plans and intent; total 0-48 (each item 0-2); higher scores = greater risk; no defined cut-offs

blocks.text: Actuarial instruments: group data from high-risk individuals is applied to the patient, giving a group risk that should be applied with caution.

blocks.title: Actuarial instruments
rows: Entirely reliant on historical factors; validated at Canadian prisons; 12 items including **PCL-R** as a subscale
Diagnoses psychopathy and informs risk assessment/treatment; 0-40 range, 0-2 per item, 20 items; cut-off 25 diagnoses psychopathy; not designed as a stand-alone actuarial risk tool
Ten-item actuarial instrument (Hanson and Thornton) for adult male sexual offenders aged 18+ at release
Manchester Self Harm Rule (Cooper et al. 2006)
Actuarial instrument for self-harm risk; high sensitivity, low specificity

blocks.title: VRAG items
rows: Absence of schizophrenia (presence counted to decrease risk)

bullets.text: Risk = likelihood of harm; cannot be eliminated, only reduced; assessment is dynamic and event-specific.
Problems predicting risk: low base rate (<1% serious violence), multifactorial, unknown interactions.
Static (fixed, historical), stable (enduring, modifiable), dynamic (fluctuating) risk factors; consider future factors too.
Clinical (subjective, only 1/3 correct), actuarial (numerical, forensic, superior for violence/sex offending), structured professional judgment (e.g. HCR-20).
Actuarial problems: historical emphasis, false positives, poor generalisation, static/stable focus; neither replaces clinical assessment.
HCR-20: 10 historical, 5 clinical, 5 risk management items; good inter-rater reliability; predicts inpatient and community violence.
SARA 20 items spousal assault; SVR-20 sexual violence; SAD PERSONS 10 factors; Beck Hopelessness 20 items; Beck SSI 24 items, 0-48.
VRAG 12 items, historical; PCL-R 20 items, 0-40, cut-off 25; Static-99 10 items; SORA 14 items; Manchester Self Harm Rule: high sensitivity, low specificity.

SADS (Kiddie-SADS for children); SCID (SCID-II axis 2)
